name: PIQA: Physical Interaction Question Answering
description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding systems. The dataset consists of multiple choice question answering pairs where a model must choose the most appropriate solution to a physical goal from two options. It contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with approximately 2K development and 3K test examples. The dataset is inspired by instructables.com and focuses on everyday situations with a preference for atypical solutions, testing knowledge of physical properties, affordances, and object manipulation.
creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
publisher: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI 2020.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) annotators who were prompted with links to instructables.com. Annotators were asked to glance at instructions from an instructable and construct two component tasks: articulate a physical goal (often centered on atypical materials) and how to achieve it, plus a permutation (trick) to their own solution which makes it invalid. Annotators were seeded with instructables drawn from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Two examples were drawn per instructable. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed from the data. This often meant that correct examples were removed that required expert level knowledge of a domain (e.g., special woodworking terminology) which should not fall under the umbrella of commonsense.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Instructions and project descriptions from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for activities ranging from cooking to car repair. Users on instructables provide images or videos detailing each step and a list of tools required.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The AFLite algorithm was used to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples from the data. AFLite performs systematic data bias reduction by discarding instances whose feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label. 5,000 examples from the original dataset were used to fine-tune BERT-Large, and the corresponding embeddings of all remaining instances were computed. AFLite uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets of the data to determine whether pre-computed embeddings are strong indicators of the correct answer option.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Goals were tokenized by Spacy. The GPT BPE tokenizer was used for solution tokenization. The longest 1% of the data was removed for analysis. Edit distance was computed over tokenized and lowercased strings with punctuation removed. Train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite. Examples were truncated at 150 tokens for model experiments, affecting 1% of the data.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk were provided with a HIT design where an instructable provided inspiration. Annotators were asked to provide: 1) a physical goal, 2) a valid solution, and 3) a trick (a permutation that sounds reasonable but is wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics). A qualification HIT was run prior to the main annotation stage where annotators had to successfully identify (>80% accuracy) well-formed and underspecified (goal, solution) pairs. Data was collected in batches and validated by other annotators for correctness. Users with low agreement were de-qualified. A diff button was included in the interface to highlight where solutions differ, which improved annotator accuracy and speed. During validation, examples with low agreement were removed.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Examples with low agreement during validation were removed from the data. Human performance was calculated by majority vote among annotators who achieved >=90% on the qualification HIT. Annotator pay averaged >$15/hr according to both self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite algorithm (for bias reduction), Spacy (for tokenization), BERT-Large (used within AFLite for embedding computation), GPT BPE tokenizer
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance AI systems' understanding of physical commonsense knowledge, which is critical for applications such as robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. The authors argue that knowledge should be learned from interaction with the world to eventually be communicated with language, and that PIQA provides a benchmark for progress towards language representations that capture knowledge traditionally only seen or experienced.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was constructed to be adversarial to BERT to reduce annotation artifacts. AFLite was applied to remove spurious biases and stylistic artifacts. Reporting bias was identified as a challenge during initial data collection: when thinking about how to achieve a goal, people most often are drawn to prototypical solutions and look for tools in the kitchen or garage, rarely considering other everyday objects. Instructables prompts were used to flatten the distribution of referenced objects and address this bias.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset focuses on physical commonsense and may not generalize to other types of commonsense reasoning. Examples requiring expert-level domain knowledge were removed during validation. The dataset was collected entirely in English. Future research may match human performance by finding large in-domain data sources and fine-tuning heavily, which the authors note is not the intended use. Models pretrained on text alone are inherently limited due to reporting bias in physical domains.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for benchmarking and evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language understanding models. It can be used for training, validation, and testing of NLP models. It is also designed as a diagnostic tool to probe the physical knowledge of deep pretrained language models. The dataset is not recommended for use cases requiring expert-level domain knowledge or non-English language understanding.
